claims.text: The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type alloy has a sharp, hysteretic, first-order magnetostructural transition.
Annealing at 600–700°C for 1–2 hours followed by cooling at 1–5°C/min will increase grain-boundary density.
The prescribed annealing treatment will alter the alloy's local defect and atomic-ordering state.
The moderate thermal budget promotes partial atomic ordering.
The moderate thermal budget produces controlled grain coarsening.
A higher density of grain-boundary-related sites can increase nucleation-site density.
Partial ordering and controlled grain coarsening increase the density and uniformity of nucleation sites for the magnetostructural transition.
More spatially dispersed nucleation broadens and makes the magnetostructural transition more gradual.
The proposed microstructural changes reduce transformation energy barriers.
Reduced transformation barriers minimize hysteretic losses.
Annealing under the specified conditions broadens the magnetocaloric transition relative to the as-deposited baseline.
Annealing under the specified conditions reduces hysteresis width during low-field magnetic cycling.
The annealing-induced microstructure enhances effective heat exchange.
The annealed samples will have improved heat-exchange capability relative to the as-deposited samples.
The annealed samples will maintain mechanical stability.
The proposed treatment will maintain low cost.
The predicted broadening and hysteresis reduction should hold under low-field cycling within the specified annealing window.
Excessive grain coarsening can eliminate the desired transition-broadening effect.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts increased grain-boundary density, while the mechanism predicts grain coarsening. Grain coarsening ordinarily reduces grain-boundary area or density unless a separate grain-refinement or boundary-generation process is specified.

Controlled grain coarsening is presented as beneficial because it increases nucleation-site density, but excessive coarsening is said to defeat the effect; no measurable grain-size window or explanation of how coarsening initially increases boundary-associated nucleation sites is supplied.
